subcategory: native Willamette Valley upland prairie perennial

planting.note: Direct sow fresh seed in fall so it experiences a natural cold, moist winter before germinating the following spring; the long taproot makes bare-root or container transplanting unreliable once plants are past their first year.

directions: Large felted gray-green leaves emerge in late winter and are quickly followed by sunflower-like yellow blooms that open alongside camas and checkerbloom in the remnant upland prairies of the Willamette Valley. The deep, woody taproot lets established plants shrug off the region's dry summers without irrigation, but it also means seedlings resent disturbance and should be sited where they can stay put for years. Grow it in lean, well-drained prairie soil rather than enriched garden beds, since excess fertility and water encourage floppy growth and rot. Cut back the coarse foliage after seed set to keep plantings tidy through the dry season.

subcategory: native Willamette Valley wet prairie annual

planting.note: Broadcast seed onto bare, moisture-retentive soil in fall; seedlings overwinter as a low rosette and bloom the following spring once the ground has been reliably saturated through winter.

directions: This low, ferny annual carpets seasonally wet swales and prairie depressions with bowl-shaped white flowers that fade to a faint pink blush and a yellow center as they age, drawing in bees and other early-season pollinators. It is the same species grown as a commercial oilseed crop on Willamette Valley farmland, so seed is easy to source even though the wild plant is restricted to naturally flooded low ground. Site it in a spot that holds winter and spring moisture but is allowed to dry by early summer, since the plant completes its life cycle and drops seed before the dry season sets in. Avoid summer watering, which only encourages weeds once the meadowfoam itself has finished for the year.

subcategory: California native vernal pool annual wildflower

planting.note: Scatter seed in fall over bare mud in a seasonally flooded basin; seed needs standing winter water to trigger germination and a spring dry-down to flower and set seed.

directions: Named for the pair of small curved horn-like appendages on its lower petal lip, this compact calicoflower forms dense, low rings of violet-blue bloom tracking the retreating shoreline of a drying Central Valley vernal pool. It is noticeably shorter and more mat-forming than the related Downingia elegans, making it well suited to the shallow outer band of a constructed vernal pool garden where water lingers only briefly. Keep it in a basin that fills with winter rain and then goes completely dry by late spring, since the plant cannot complete its cycle under constant irrigation. Pair it with other vernal pool specialists rather than ordinary bedding annuals, which cannot tolerate the same flood-then-drought regime.

subcategory: California native vernal pool margin annual wildflower

planting.note: Direct sow in fall onto the drier upper margin of a vernal pool basin or seasonal swale, where winter rain keeps soil moist but not standing; plants bloom as the margin begins to dry in spring.

directions: Clusters of small, fragrant white flowers with a yellow eye open along the upper, less saturated margin of Central Valley vernal pools, filling the band between the open water of the pool bottom and the surrounding dry grassland. Because it tolerates less flooding than true pool-bottom species, it works well along the rim of a backyard vernal pool feature or in a seasonally damp low spot that never holds standing water for long. Give it moist winter and spring soil, then let the site dry out by early summer so the plant can finish setting seed. It self-sows readily where the flood-then-drought cycle is maintained year after year.

subcategory: California native vernal pool margin annual legume

planting.note: Direct sow in fall on the drying margin of a vernal pool basin or seasonally damp grassy flat; no pretreatment is needed, and plants complete their cycle before the ground dries completely in late spring.

directions: This low-growing native clover gets its common name from the inflated, balloon-like calyx that swells around each small pink-and-white flower head after bloom, a feature that sets it apart from the weedy European clovers found in the same fields. Like other vernal pool margin annuals it fixes nitrogen into the thin, seasonally saturated soils where it grows, then sets seed and dies back completely as the ground dries for summer. Use it along the damp fringe of a vernal pool garden or seasonal swale rather than in a regularly irrigated lawn or bed, since summer water keeps the dormant seed from resetting for the following winter. It mixes naturally with popcornflower and other small vernal pool margin annuals rather than forming solid stands on its own.
